study.title: Acts 4 The Gospel Faced with Opposition and Church Life in Communion
study.overview: Acts 4 shows that the expansion of the gospel does not advance without resistance, but is not paralyzed by it either. Peter and John are imprisoned because they announce, in the name of Jesus, the resurrection of the dead, and then are interrogated by the religious authorities. At the center of the apostolic response is a double conviction: the healing of the crippled man came by the name of Jesus Christ, crucified and risen, and there is no salvation in any other. The chapter then passes from opposition to prayer: the church interprets the threat to the light of the Scriptures, asks boldness to continue speaking the word, receives renewal by the Holy Spirit and manifests unity, generosity and practical care for those in need. The end of the chapter presents Barnabas as a concrete example of this delivery, by selling a field and placing value at the apostles' feet.

outline.title: Prison, opposition and growth of the number of believers
outline.explanation: While the apostles still spoke to the people, priests, the temple officer and Sadducees interrupt them, because preaching about Jesus and the resurrection bothers them. Peter and John are imprisoned, but the word is not prevented: many believe, and the number of men reaches about five thousand.

outline.title: The interrogation and the exclusive confession of salvation in Jesus
outline.explanation: The next day, leaders, elders, and scribes examine the apostles. Full of the Holy Spirit, Peter states that man's healing came by the name of Jesus Christ, the Nazarene, crucified and risen. He declares that Jesus is the stone rejected by the builders and that there is no salvation in any other name given among human beings.

outline.title: Religious authority recognizes the sign, but tries to silence the message
outline.explanation: The leaders are surprised at the boldness of men considered uneducated, but realize that they had been with Jesus. Since they cannot deny the miracle, they decide to threaten them to prevent disclosure. Peter and John answer that it is necessary to judge whether it is fair to hear more of men than God, and they claim that they cannot fail to speak of what they have seen and heard.

outline.title: The prayer of the church, the response of the Spirit and the generous communion
outline.explanation: Freed, the apostles report everything to the brethren, who oram unanimously, recognizing God's rule over opposition against Jesus. They ask boldness to preach and signs by the name of Jesus. God responds by filling all of the Holy Spirit. The community remains united in mind and heart, shares its possessions, bears witness to the resurrection with great power and grace, supplies the needy and exemplifies it in Barnabas, which sells a property and delivers value to the apostles.

study.context: The chapter takes place in Jerusalem, in an environment of confrontation with the Jewish leaders. The text mentions priests, the temple officer, Sadducees, chiefs, elders, scribes, and the supreme council, which shows a scenario of formal religious authority. By the notes provided, the Sadducees reacted in a special way because the preaching of the resurrection threatened their thought. The church assembly also appears in prayer, gathered around the apostles, with a strong sense of community.
study.theology: Acts 4 teaches that human opposition does not invalidate the work of God; on the contrary, it can serve to show the faithfulness of the disciples and divine sovereignty. The healing of the sick man points to Jesus as the center of God's saving action, and the resurrection is presented as a decisive fact for the Christian message. Peter's statement in 4:12 is a strong affirmation of exclusivity: salvation is not found in other names, means or authorities, but only in Christ. At the same time, the chapter unites truth and practice: the church prays for boldness, not by escaping; seeks fidelity, not comfort; and expresses new life in concrete generosity, sharing and care of the needy. The final prayer also shows that the opposition against Jesus was not an accident outside of God's control, but part of what his hand and counsel had determined, without withdrawing the guilt of those who acted against the Anointed.

scholarViews.insight: Persecution is a recurring experience of God's people, and the chapter shows that the Holy Spirit empowers the disciples to witness even in the midst of opposition.
Healing and preaching were treated as a crime by the leaders, although they were the best service the apostles could render to God and people.
Peter's statement about the name of Jesus emphasizes that there is no salvation in any other, either for the body or for the soul.

questions: What does this chapter reveal about the difference between impressing religious authorities and obeying God faithfully?
In what sense does our church or community need to ask more boldly and less comfort when praying?
How does Barnabas' generosity confront our tendency to retain goods, time and attention only to ourselves?
study.practice: Read Acts 4 in prayer and identify an area where you are afraid to speak of Christ clearly. Ask God boldness for a concrete conversation this week. Then choose a real need around you - someone sick, financially or emotionally overwhelmed - and practice a specific, discreet and measurable help. If you participate in a Christian community, encourage the church to pray not only for relief but for the courage to remain faithful to the word.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided allow to safely affirm the opposition of the leaders, the importance of the Sadducees in the face of the preaching of the resurrection, the exclusivity of salvation in Jesus and the example of Barnabas. However, they do not provide wider historical details on exact dates, specific political arrangements or linguistic explanations beyond the translations already given in the text itself and in the notes. Therefore, the study avoids any external information not supported.
